# Finite Element Approximation {#sec-fem-approximation}

```{=latex}
\chaptershorttitle{Finite Element Approximation}
```

The variational problems developed in Chapters 3 and 4 are posed in
infinite-dimensional function spaces. They provide the mathematical problem that we
want to solve, but they do not yet provide a finite system of equations that can be
given to a computer. The finite element method makes this transition by replacing the
continuous trial and test spaces with finite-dimensional spaces of piecewise
polynomial functions.

This chapter develops that construction in full. We begin with the Galerkin method,
define a finite element on one cell, join the cellwise functions into a global
conforming space, and then derive the element matrices, assembly operation, and
treatment of prescribed boundary values. The heat-conduction and linear-elasticity
problems from Chapter 4 will provide the main examples. The final section connects
each mathematical object to its implementation in FEniCSx. Standard treatments of
these topics may be found in [@becker-carey-oden1981; @jog;
@larson-bengzon2010].

## From the continuous problem to a discrete problem {#sec-fem-galerkin}

Consider the homogeneous variational problem

$$
\text{find }u\in\Vzero
\quad\text{such that}\quad
a(u,v)=\ell(v)
\quad\forall v\in\Vzero,
$$ {#eq-fem-continuous-problem}

where $\Vzero$ is an infinite-dimensional function space. Suppose that
$\mathcal V_{h,0}$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $\Vzero$. The subscript $h$
indicates that the space is associated with a mesh having characteristic cell size
$h$.

::: {#def-fem-conforming-galerkin}
## Conforming Galerkin approximation

Let $\mathcal V_{h,0}\subset\Vzero$ be finite-dimensional. The conforming Galerkin
approximation of @eq-fem-continuous-problem is

$$
\boxed{
\text{find }\uh\in\mathcal V_{h,0}
\quad\text{such that}\quad
a(\uh,\vh)=\ell(\vh)
\quad\forall\vh\in\mathcal V_{h,0}.}
$$ {#eq-fem-discrete-galerkin}
:::

The word *conforming* refers to the inclusion
$\mathcal V_{h,0}\subset\Vzero$. Thus every discrete trial and test function is also
an admissible function for the continuous variational problem. We do not derive a new
weak form after choosing the mesh; we restrict the trial and test functions in the
existing weak form to finite-dimensional spaces.

Let $\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N\}$ be a basis for $\mathcal V_{h,0}$. Every
$\uh\in\mathcal V_{h,0}$ has a unique representation

$$
\uh=\sum_{j=1}^N U_j\phi_j,
$$ {#eq-fem-basis-expansion}

where $U_j$ are unknown coefficients. Because @eq-fem-discrete-galerkin is linear
in the test function, it is enough to impose the equation for each basis function
$\phi_i$. Substitution of @eq-fem-basis-expansion gives

$$
\sum_{j=1}^N a(\phi_j,\phi_i)U_j=\ell(\phi_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
$$ {#eq-fem-basis-equations}

Therefore, the discrete problem is the linear system

$$
\boxed{\bm K\bm U=\bm F},
\qquad
K_{ij}=a(\phi_j,\phi_i),
\qquad
F_i=\ell(\phi_i).
$$ {#eq-fem-global-system}

The row index $i$ is associated with the test function, and the column index $j$
with the trial function. If $a$ is symmetric, then $\bm K$ is symmetric. If $a$ is
also coercive on $\Vzero$, then for every nonzero coefficient vector $\bm Z$,

$$
\bm Z\cdot\bm K\bm Z
=a\left(\sum_i Z_i\phi_i,\sum_j Z_j\phi_j\right)>0,
$$

so $\bm K$ is positive definite.

::: {#exr-fem-basis-system}
## From the Galerkin equation to a matrix system

Starting from @eq-fem-discrete-galerkin, use @eq-fem-basis-expansion and choose
$\vh=\phi_i$ to derive @eq-fem-basis-equations. Then show that symmetry of $a$
implies $K_{ij}=K_{ji}$.
:::

## Meshes and cells {#sec-fem-meshes}

A finite element space is built over a subdivision of the domain. Let
$\Om\subset\R^d$ be a bounded domain. A mesh $\Th$ is a finite collection of open
cells $K$ such that the interiors of distinct cells do not overlap and

$$
\overline{\Om}=\bigcup_{K\in\Th}\overline K.
$$ {#eq-fem-mesh-cover}

In one dimension the cells are intervals. Common cells in two dimensions are
triangles and quadrilaterals; in three dimensions they include tetrahedra and
hexahedra. A boundary of codimension one is called a *facet*: an endpoint in one
dimension, an edge in two dimensions, and a face in three dimensions.

For a conforming mesh, the closures of two distinct cells are either disjoint or
meet in a complete shared vertex, edge, or face. Hanging nodes, in which a vertex of
one cell lies in the interior of a neighboring facet, require additional constraints
and will not be considered in this chapter.

The diameter of a cell and the mesh size are denoted by

$$
h_K=\sup_{\bx,\bm y\in K}\lVert\bx-\bm y\rVert_2,
\qquad
h=\max_{K\in\Th}h_K.
$$ {#eq-fem-cell-mesh-size}

Reducing $h$ produces smaller cells, but cell size is not the only relevant geometric
property. Extremely thin or distorted cells can lead to poor approximation and
ill-conditioned algebraic systems. Quantitative assumptions on mesh shape will be
introduced in Chapter 6 when error estimates are developed.

::: {.remark}
## Vertices, nodes, and degrees of freedom

A *vertex* is a geometric corner of a cell. A *node* is a point used to define a
nodal finite element. A *degree of freedom* is a linear measurement of a finite
element function. These terms coincide for first-order Lagrange elements, but not in
general. A higher-order element has nodes in addition to its vertices, and some
finite elements use edge or cell moments rather than point values.
:::

## The finite element on one cell {#sec-fem-element-triple}

The local construction must specify the cell, the functions allowed on that cell,
and the information used to determine one such function.

::: {#def-fem-element-triple}
## Finite element

A finite element is a triple $(K,\mathcal P,\mathcal N)$ in which

1. $K$ is a cell;
2. $\mathcal P$ is a finite-dimensional space of functions on $K$; and
3. $\mathcal N=\{N_1,\ldots,N_m\}$ is a basis for the dual space
   $\mathcal P^*$.

The linear functionals $N_i:\mathcal P\to\R$ are the local degrees of freedom.
:::

Since $\mathcal N$ is a basis for $\mathcal P^*$, the degrees of freedom determine
each $p\in\mathcal P$ uniquely. Equivalently,

$$
N_i(p)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p=0.
$$ {#eq-fem-unisolvence}

This property is called *unisolvence*. It guarantees the existence of a unique local
nodal basis $\{\phi_1^K,\ldots,\phi_m^K\}$ satisfying

$$
N_i(\phi_j^K)=\delta_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-fem-local-nodal-basis}

Consequently, every $p\in\mathcal P$ can be reconstructed from its degrees of
freedom:

$$
p=\sum_{j=1}^m N_j(p)\phi_j^K.
$$ {#eq-fem-local-interpolation}

### Polynomial spaces

The space $\mathbb P_p(K)$ contains polynomials of total degree at most $p$. In two
dimensions,

$$
\mathbb P_p(K)
=\operatorname{span}\{x_1^i x_2^j:i,j\ge 0,\ i+j\le p\},
\qquad
\dim\mathbb P_p(K)=\frac{(p+1)(p+2)}{2}.
$$ {#eq-fem-Pp-space}

On quadrilateral cells, the tensor-product space $\mathbb Q_p$ is commonly used:

$$
\mathbb Q_p(K)
=\operatorname{span}\{x_1^i x_2^j:0\le i,j\le p\},
\qquad
\dim\mathbb Q_p(K)=(p+1)^2.
$$ {#eq-fem-Qp-space}

For example, $x_1x_2$ belongs to $\mathbb Q_1$ but not to $\mathbb P_1$. The order
$p$ controls the local polynomial degree and is distinct from the mesh size $h$.

### Lagrange elements on intervals and triangles

For an interval $K=[x_a,x_b]$, the linear Lagrange element uses
$\mathcal P=\mathbb P_1(K)$ and the endpoint values

$$
N_1(p)=p(x_a),
\qquad
N_2(p)=p(x_b).
$$

The corresponding basis functions are

$$
\phi_1^K(x)=\frac{x_b-x}{x_b-x_a},
\qquad
\phi_2^K(x)=\frac{x-x_a}{x_b-x_a}.
$$ {#eq-fem-linear-interval-basis}

They satisfy $\phi_i^K(x_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and
$\phi_1^K+\phi_2^K=1$.

For a triangle with vertices $\bx_1,\bx_2,\bx_3$, the linear Lagrange element uses
$\mathbb P_1(K)$ and the three vertex values. Its basis functions are the barycentric
coordinates $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, defined by

$$
\lambda_i(\bx_j)=\delta_{ij},
\qquad
\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1.
$$ {#eq-fem-barycentric-properties}

Every affine function $p\in\mathbb P_1(K)$ is then represented as

$$
p(\bx)=\sum_{i=1}^3 p(\bx_i)\lambda_i(\bx).
$$ {#eq-fem-triangle-affine-reproduction}

::: {#exr-fem-reference-triangle-basis}
## Basis functions on the reference triangle

Let $\widehat K$ have vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,1)$. Show that the linear
Lagrange basis is

$$
\widehat\phi_1=1-\xi-\eta,
\qquad
\widehat\phi_2=\xi,
\qquad
\widehat\phi_3=\eta.
$$

Verify both @eq-fem-barycentric-properties and
@eq-fem-triangle-affine-reproduction.
:::

On the reference square $\widehat K=[-1,1]^2$, the four $\mathbb Q_1$ basis
functions are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\phi_1&=\tfrac14(1-\xi)(1-\eta), &
\widehat\phi_2&=\tfrac14(1+\xi)(1-\eta),\\
\widehat\phi_3&=\tfrac14(1+\xi)(1+\eta), &
\widehat\phi_4&=\tfrac14(1-\xi)(1+\eta).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fem-Q1-square-basis}

These functions are bilinear: each is linear in $\xi$ when $\eta$ is fixed and
linear in $\eta$ when $\xi$ is fixed.

::: {#exr-fem-quadratic-interval}
## Quadratic Lagrange element

On $[-1,1]$, use the nodes $-1$, $0$, and $1$ to construct the three quadratic
Lagrange basis functions. Verify the nodal property and show that their sum is one.
:::

## From local elements to a global conforming space {#sec-fem-global-space}

For a conforming mesh of intervals or triangles, the scalar Lagrange space of order
$p$ is

$$
\Vh=
\{v_h\in C(\overline\Om):v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_p(K)
\text{ for every }K\in\Th\}.
$$ {#eq-fem-global-lagrange-space}

Mapped tensor-product polynomials are used in the corresponding quadrilateral and
hexahedral spaces. Because functions in @eq-fem-global-lagrange-space are continuous
and have square-integrable cellwise gradients, $\Vh\subset H^1(\Om)$. Their
gradients may jump across cell facets; membership in $H^1(\Om)$ does not require the
gradient to be continuous.

The global continuity is obtained by identifying degrees of freedom shared by
neighboring cells. Let

$$
I_K:\{1,\ldots,m_K\}\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,N\}
$$

map local degree of freedom $a$ on cell $K$ to its global number $I_K(a)$. The
restriction of a global finite element function to $K$ can then be written

$$
v_h|_K=\sum_{a=1}^{m_K}V_{I_K(a)}\phi_a^K.
$$ {#eq-fem-local-global-expansion}

For a one-dimensional mesh $x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n$, the global basis function
associated with an interior node $x_i$ is the familiar hat function

$$
\phi_i(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x-x_{i-1}}{x_i-x_{i-1}}, & x\in[x_{i-1},x_i],\\[6pt]
\dfrac{x_{i+1}-x}{x_{i+1}-x_i}, & x\in[x_i,x_{i+1}],\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-fem-hat-function}

Its support contains only the two cells meeting at $x_i$. This local support is the
reason that finite element matrices are sparse.

::: {#exr-fem-two-cell-continuity}
## Joining two linear elements

Let $K_1=[0,1]$ and $K_2=[1,2]$. Write a general linear polynomial on each cell.
Determine the condition on their four endpoint coefficients that makes the resulting
piecewise function continuous at $x=1$. Then express the function using three global
nodal values.
:::

## Reference cells and geometric mappings {#sec-fem-reference-maps}

It would be wasteful to derive basis functions and quadrature rules separately on
every cell. Instead, they are defined once on a reference cell $\widehat K$ and
mapped to each physical cell $K$.

For an affine simplex, the geometric map has the form

$$
\bx=F_K(\widehat{\bx})=\bm B_K\widehat{\bx}+\bb_K,
$$ {#eq-fem-affine-map}

where $\bm B_K$ is nonsingular. A scalar reference basis function
$\widehat\phi_a$ defines a physical basis function by

$$
\phi_a^K(\bx)=\widehat\phi_a(F_K^{-1}(\bx)).
$$ {#eq-fem-scalar-pullback}

The chain rule and change-of-variables formula give

$$
\grad_{\bx}\phi_a^K
=\bm B_K^{-T}\grad_{\widehat{\bx}}\widehat\phi_a,
$$ {#eq-fem-gradient-map}

and

$$
\int_K q(\bx)\,\dd\bx
=\int_{\widehat K}q(F_K(\widehat{\bx}))
\left|\det\bm B_K\right|\,\dd\widehat{\bx}.
$$ {#eq-fem-change-variables}

For example, the map from $[-1,1]$ to $[x_a,x_b]$ is

$$
x=\frac{x_a+x_b}{2}+\frac{x_b-x_a}{2}\xi,
\qquad
\frac{\dd x}{\dd\xi}=\frac{x_b-x_a}{2}.
$$ {#eq-fem-interval-map}

### Isoparametric geometry

For quadrilateral, hexahedral, and curved cells, the geometry can be represented
using the same type of basis functions used for the field approximation:

$$
\bx=F_K(\widehat{\bx})
=\sum_{a=1}^{n_g}\bx_a\widehat\phi_a(\widehat{\bx}).
$$ {#eq-fem-isoparametric-map}

This is an *isoparametric* map. Its Jacobian matrix

$$
\bm J_K(\widehat{\bx})
=\frac{\partial\bx}{\partial\widehat{\bx}}
$$

generally varies over the cell. Equations @eq-fem-gradient-map and
@eq-fem-change-variables then hold pointwise with $\bm B_K$ replaced by
$\bm J_K(\widehat{\bx})$. A valid orientation-preserving cell map must satisfy
$\det\bm J_K>0$ throughout $\widehat K$.

::: {#exr-fem-triangle-map}
## Mapping a reference triangle

Let the physical triangle have vertices $\bx_1$, $\bx_2$, and $\bx_3$. Starting
from the basis in @exr-fem-reference-triangle-basis, show that

$$
F_K(\xi,\eta)=\bx_1+(\bx_2-\bx_1)\xi+(\bx_3-\bx_1)\eta.
$$

Compute $\bm B_K$ and show that the area of $K$ is
$|\det\bm B_K|/2$.
:::

## Numerical quadrature {#sec-fem-quadrature}

The integrals defining element matrices and vectors are evaluated numerically. A
quadrature rule on the reference cell has points $\widehat{\bx}_q$ and weights $w_q$
such that

$$
\int_{\widehat K}\widehat q(\widehat{\bx})\,\dd\widehat{\bx}
\approx\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}w_q\widehat q(\widehat{\bx}_q).
$$ {#eq-fem-reference-quadrature}

Combining this rule with the geometric map gives

$$
\int_K q(\bx)\,\dd\bx
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}w_q\,q(F_K(\widehat{\bx}_q))
\left|\det\bm J_K(\widehat{\bx}_q)\right|.
$$ {#eq-fem-physical-quadrature}

A quadrature rule has degree of exactness $r$ if it integrates every polynomial of
degree at most $r$ exactly. An $n_q$-point Gauss rule in one dimension is exact
through degree $2n_q-1$. Tensor products of one-dimensional rules are commonly used
on quadrilaterals and hexahedra; separate rules are used on simplices.

The required quadrature order depends on the complete integrand. For an affine cell,
constant diffusion coefficient, and $\mathbb P_p$ basis, the product
$\grad\phi_i\cdot\grad\phi_j$ has degree at most $2p-2$. Variable coefficients,
nonlinear constitutive equations, and nonaffine geometric maps change this count.

::: {.warning}
## Underintegration

A quadrature rule with insufficient accuracy changes the element matrix. In some
problems this can introduce rank deficiency or nonphysical deformation modes. The
quadrature order should therefore be chosen from the actual integrand, not from the
basis degree alone.
:::

::: {#exr-fem-gauss-rule}
## Two-point Gauss rule

The two-point Gauss rule on $[-1,1]$ uses points
$\xi=\pm1/\sqrt{3}$ and unit weights. Verify that it is exact for
$1,\xi,\xi^2,$ and $\xi^3$, but not for $\xi^4$. Then use
@eq-fem-interval-map to write the corresponding rule on $[x_a,x_b]$.
:::

## Element matrices and assembly {#sec-fem-assembly}

The global variational forms are sums of cell and boundary-facet integrals. For
example,

$$
a(u_h,v_h)
=\sum_{K\in\Th}a_K(u_h,v_h)
+\sum_{E\subset\partial\Om}a_E(u_h,v_h).
$$ {#eq-fem-form-decomposition}

On a cell $K$, define the element matrix and vector by

$$
K_{ab}^K=a_K(\phi_b^K,\phi_a^K),
\qquad
F_a^K=\ell_K(\phi_a^K),
\qquad a,b=1,\ldots,m_K.
$$ {#eq-fem-element-matrix-vector}

The local-to-global map $I_K$ determines where these entries belong:

$$
K_{I_K(a),I_K(b)}\mathrel{+}=K_{ab}^K,
\qquad
F_{I_K(a)}\mathrel{+}=F_a^K.
$$ {#eq-fem-assembly-operation}

The notation $\mathrel{+}=$ means that contributions are added to entries that may
already contain contributions from neighboring cells. Since two global basis
functions interact only when their supports overlap, most entries of $\bm K$ are
zero.

### A complete one-dimensional calculation

Consider

$$
-\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\left(k\frac{\dd u}{\dd x}\right)=f
\quad\text{in }(0,L),
\qquad
u(0)=u(L)=0,
$$ {#eq-fem-1d-diffusion}

with constant $k>0$. On an element $K=[x_a,x_b]$ of length $h_K$, the derivatives
of the basis functions in @eq-fem-linear-interval-basis are $-1/h_K$ and $1/h_K$.
The element stiffness matrix is therefore

$$
\bm K^K
=\int_K k
\begin{bmatrix}\phi_1'\\\phi_2'\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\phi_1'&\phi_2'\end{bmatrix}\dd x
=\frac{k}{h_K}
\begin{bmatrix}
1&-1\\
-1&1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-fem-1d-element-stiffness}

If $f$ is constant on $K$, its element load vector is

$$
\bm F^K
=\int_K f
\begin{bmatrix}\phi_1\\\phi_2\end{bmatrix}\dd x
=\frac{f h_K}{2}
\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-fem-1d-element-load}

For three equal elements, assembly of the stiffness matrices before imposition of
the endpoint values gives

$$
\bm K=\frac{k}{h}
\begin{bmatrix}
1&-1&0&0\\
-1&2&-1&0\\
0&-1&2&-1\\
0&0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-fem-1d-assembled-stiffness}

The diagonal entries at the two interior nodes contain two cell contributions,
whereas those at the endpoints contain one.

::: {#exr-fem-two-element-assembly}
## Assembly on a nonuniform mesh

Divide $[0,L]$ into $K_1=[0,x_1]$ and $K_2=[x_1,L]$, with lengths $h_1$ and
$h_2$. Let the diffusion coefficient have constant values $k_1$ and $k_2$ on the
two cells. Derive both element matrices and assemble the $3\times3$ global matrix.
:::

## Prescribed boundary values {#sec-fem-essential-bc}

Natural and Robin boundary conditions already appear as boundary integrals in the
variational problem. Prescribed, or essential, boundary values instead restrict the
finite element trial and test spaces. For homogeneous data,

$$
\mathcal V_{h,0}=\Vh\cap\Vzero.
$$ {#eq-fem-homogeneous-test-space}

For prescribed data $g$, let $g_h$ denote its discrete representation on
$\Gamma_D$. The trial space is

$$
\mathcal U_{h,g}
=\{w_h\in\Vh:w_h=g_h\text{ on }\Gamma_D\},
$$ {#eq-fem-nonhomogeneous-trial-space}

and the discrete problem is

$$
\text{find }u_h\in\mathcal U_{h,g}
\quad\text{such that}\quad
a(u_h,v_h)=\ell(v_h)
\quad\forall v_h\in\mathcal V_{h,0}.
$$ {#eq-fem-nonhomogeneous-discrete-problem}

At the algebraic level, divide the coefficients into free values $\bm U_f$ and
prescribed values $\bm U_p$. The assembled system has the block form

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\bm K_{ff}&\bm K_{fp}\\
\bm K_{pf}&\bm K_{pp}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\bm U_f\\\bm U_p\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\bm F_f\\\bm F_p\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $\bm U_p$ is known, the equations associated with the free coefficients are

$$
\boxed{\bm K_{ff}\bm U_f
=\bm F_f-\bm K_{fp}\bm U_p.}
$$ {#eq-fem-eliminated-system}

The term $-\bm K_{fp}\bm U_p$ is the algebraic effect of the prescribed boundary
values. Software may impose these values by elimination or by equivalent row and
column modifications. Any such modification must include the corresponding change
to the right-hand side.

::: {#exr-fem-prescribed-values}
## Prescribed endpoint values

For the matrix in @eq-fem-1d-assembled-stiffness, suppose $U_0=T_0$ and
$U_3=T_L$ are prescribed. Write the $2\times2$ system for the unknowns $U_1$ and
$U_2$, including the contributions from $T_0$ and $T_L$ on the right-hand side.
:::

## Scalar heat-conduction matrices {#sec-fem-heat-matrices}

For the steady heat-conduction problem in @eq-model-steady-heat-weak, the local
conduction matrix on a cell $K$ is

$$
K_{ab}^{K,\mathrm{cond}}
=\int_K k\grad\phi_a^K\cdot\grad\phi_b^K\,\dd\bx.
$$ {#eq-fem-heat-conduction-matrix}

A Robin boundary facet $E\subset\Gamma_R$ contributes

$$
K_{ab}^{E,\mathrm{conv}}
=\int_E h_c\phi_a^K\phi_b^K\,\dd s.
$$ {#eq-fem-heat-convection-matrix}

The corresponding local load contributions are

$$
F_a^{K,\mathrm{src}}=\int_K r\phi_a^K\,\dd\bx,
\qquad
F_a^{E,\mathrm{flux}}=-\int_E\overline q\phi_a^K\,\dd s,
\qquad
F_a^{E,\mathrm{amb}}=\int_E h_cT_\infty\phi_a^K\,\dd s.
$$ {#eq-fem-heat-load-vectors}

The minus sign in the flux term follows the outward-flux convention established in
Chapter 4. After cell and boundary-facet contributions are assembled, prescribed
temperatures are imposed as described in @sec-fem-essential-bc.

::: {#exr-fem-heat-term-classification}
## Heat-conduction element terms

For each term in @eq-fem-heat-conduction-matrix--@eq-fem-heat-load-vectors, state
whether it contributes to the global matrix or the global right-hand side, and
whether it is integrated over a cell or a boundary facet.
:::

## Linear-elasticity matrices {#sec-fem-elasticity-matrices}

For displacement, the scalar Lagrange space is used componentwise:

$$
\boldsymbol{\mathcal V}_h=[\Vh]^d.
$$ {#eq-fem-vector-space}

If $\phi_a$ is a scalar nodal basis function, then
$\phi_a\bm e_1,\ldots,\phi_a\bm e_d$ are vector basis functions. Thus a mesh node has
$d$ displacement degrees of freedom. For local node $a$ and component $\alpha$, set

$$
\boldsymbol\phi_{a\alpha}=\phi_a^K\bm e_\alpha.
$$

Using the linear-elasticity bilinear form from @eq-model-linear-elasticity-forms,
the element stiffness entries are

$$
K_{a\alpha,b\beta}^{K,\mathrm{el}}
=\int_K
\beps(\boldsymbol\phi_{a\alpha}):\mathbb C:
\beps(\boldsymbol\phi_{b\beta})\,\dd\bx.
$$ {#eq-fem-elasticity-element-stiffness}

The body-force and traction contributions are

$$
F_{a\alpha}^{K,\mathrm{body}}
=\int_K b_\alpha\phi_a^K\,\dd\bx,
\qquad
F_{a\alpha}^{E,\mathrm{trac}}
=\int_E \overline t_\alpha\phi_a^K\,\dd s.
$$ {#eq-fem-elasticity-load-vectors}

In two dimensions, the engineering-strain vector introduced in Chapter 4 can be
written for a nodal displacement
$\phi_a^K\bm d_a$ as

$$
\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{V,a}=\bm B_a\bm d_a,
\qquad
\bm B_a=
\begin{bmatrix}
\phi_{a,1}&0\\
0&\phi_{a,2}\\
\phi_{a,2}&\phi_{a,1}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-fem-elasticity-B-matrix}

With the same Voigt ordering for $\bm C_V$ as in
@eq-model-voigt-constitutive-law, a $2\times2$ block of the element stiffness
matrix is

$$
\bm K_{ab}^{K,\mathrm{el}}
=\int_K\bm B_a^T\bm C_V\bm B_b\,\dd\bx.
$$ {#eq-fem-elasticity-voigt-stiffness}

The tensor expression @eq-fem-elasticity-element-stiffness is primary. The matrix
$\bm B_a$ is a convenient implementation of the same strain operation after a
particular Voigt ordering has been fixed. Essential boundary conditions may be
applied to all displacement components at a node or to selected components only.

::: {#exr-fem-triangle-elasticity-basis}
## Vector basis on a linear triangle

For a two-dimensional linear triangle with scalar basis
$\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$, list its six vector basis functions. Use
@eq-fem-elasticity-B-matrix to compute the engineering-strain vector associated with
$\phi_2\bm e_1$ and with $\phi_2\bm e_2$.
:::

## The finite element construction in FEniCSx {#sec-fem-fenicsx}

FEniCSx follows the same construction developed above. Basix defines finite elements
and tabulates their basis functions; UFL represents variational forms; DOLFINx
creates meshes, function spaces, boundary conditions, and assembled operators; and
PETSc stores and solves the resulting algebraic systems.

| Mathematical object | FEniCSx representation |
|---|---|
| mesh $\Th$ | `dolfinx.mesh.Mesh` |
| finite element space $\Vh$ | `dolfinx.fem.FunctionSpace` |
| trial and test symbols | `ufl.TrialFunction`, `ufl.TestFunction` |
| finite element field $u_h$ | `dolfinx.fem.Function` |
| $a(u_h,v_h)$ and $\ell(v_h)$ | UFL forms |
| prescribed boundary values | `dolfinx.fem.DirichletBC` |
| $\bm K$, $\bm F$, and the solver | PETSc objects |

The following program solves a manufactured Poisson problem on the unit square. The
exact solution $u=\sin(\pi x_1)\sin(\pi x_2)$ satisfies
$-\Delta u=2\pi^2u$ and is zero on the boundary.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"}
from mpi4py import MPI
from petsc4py import PETSc
import numpy as np
import ufl
from dolfinx import fem, mesh
from dolfinx.fem.petsc import LinearProblem

# Mesh and scalar Lagrange space
domain = mesh.create_unit_square(MPI.COMM_WORLD, 32, 32)
V = fem.functionspace(domain, ("Lagrange", 1))

# Trial function, test function, and manufactured data
u = ufl.TrialFunction(V)
v = ufl.TestFunction(V)
x = ufl.SpatialCoordinate(domain)
u_exact = ufl.sin(np.pi * x[0]) * ufl.sin(np.pi * x[1])
f = 2.0 * np.pi**2 * u_exact

# Variational forms
a = ufl.inner(ufl.grad(u), ufl.grad(v)) * ufl.dx
L = f * v * ufl.dx

# Homogeneous values on the entire boundary
fdim = domain.topology.dim - 1
facets = mesh.locate_entities_boundary(
    domain, fdim, lambda x: np.full(x.shape[1], True, dtype=bool)
)
dofs = fem.locate_dofs_topological(V, fdim, facets)
bc = fem.dirichletbc(PETSc.ScalarType(0.0), dofs, V)

# Assembly and linear solution
problem = LinearProblem(
    a,
    L,
    bcs=[bc],
    petsc_options_prefix="poisson_",
    petsc_options={"ksp_type": "preonly", "pc_type": "lu"},
)
uh = problem.solve()

# Global L2 error
error_form = fem.form((uh - u_exact) ** 2 * ufl.dx)
error_local = fem.assemble_scalar(error_form)
error_L2 = np.sqrt(domain.comm.allreduce(error_local, op=MPI.SUM))
print(f"L2 error: {error_L2:.6e}")
```
:::


The calls that define `a` and `L` state the variational problem. During assembly,
FEniCSx performs the reference-cell tabulation, geometric mapping, quadrature, and
local-to-global accumulation described in the preceding sections.

Before interpreting a numerical result, several elementary checks should be made:

1. verify that the intended boundary facets and degrees of freedom were selected;
2. check the sign and units of every source and boundary term;
3. compare with a manufactured or analytically solvable problem when possible;
4. repeat the calculation on successively refined meshes; and
5. for parallel computations, compare a small problem with its serial result.

Mesh refinement should cause an accurate and consistent calculation to approach a
stable result. The theoretical tools used to prove convergence and predict rates are
developed in Chapter 6.

## Chapter summary {#sec-fem-summary}

The finite element method restricts a continuous variational problem to
finite-dimensional trial and test spaces. A mesh divides the domain into cells, and
the triple $(K,\mathcal P,\mathcal N)$ defines the approximation on each cell.
Shared degrees of freedom join the local functions into a conforming global space.
Reference-cell maps and quadrature make the element calculations reusable, while
the local-to-global map assembles the element matrices and vectors into a sparse
system. Prescribed boundary values restrict the discrete trial and test spaces and
must also be accounted for in the algebraic right-hand side. These same operations
produce the heat-conduction and elasticity systems and are carried out directly by
FEniCSx. Chapter 6 will examine the approximation error and its dependence on mesh
size and polynomial order.
